item.title: Agroforestry and Intercropping Practices
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /cocoa_book/02_cocoa_cultivation/02_intercropping_practices/ -

Overview

Cocoa is commonly cultivated in agroforestry systems, where it grows under the partial shade of taller trees. Shade is especially important during the early stages of cocoa growth, helping young plants establish more successfully by reducing heat and water stress.

In many cocoa-growing regions, especially in West Africa, farmers aim for medium to low shade levels, where cocoa dominates the understory and shade trees are scattered throughout the plot. For example, in Ghana, the Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) recommends maintaining 16 to 18 large shade trees per hectare, spaced roughly 24×24 meters, to provide an optimal 30–40% shade cover.

Cocoa is also frequently intercropped with other useful species. These can include fast-growing shade providers like banana or plantain, tall palms like coconut, or other perennials such as citrus, avocado, and safou. These intercropping systems provide food, income, or ecological benefits while shaping the overall structure of the cocoa landscape.

item.title: The Coffee Life Cycle
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/02_life_cycle/ -

Overview

The life cycle of a coffee tree begins in a nursery before being transplanted into the field. Once planted, it typically takes 3 to 4 years for the young coffee trees to mature and start bearing fruit. During this maturation period, coffee is often intercropped with other commercially valuable crops such as banana, plantain, or passion fruit vines. These companion crops provide shade and generate income for farmers while the coffee trees develop.

Upon reaching maturity, coffee trees are usually pruned annually after the harvest to maintain their structure and productivity, although the frequency of this practice is not universal.

After nine to ten years   or as early as five to six years in Colombia   coffee trees are commonly stumped, cutting back the trunk to its base to encourage regrowth and to sustain high yields. This rejuvenation process takes about a year. After approximately twenty years, the productivity of coffee trees declines significantly, prompting their removal and replacement with new seedlings.

item.title: Cash Crops
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/01_coffee_gallery/02_confounding_samples/03_industrial/ -

Overview

Plantation cash crops are widely grown in tropical regions and often share structural similarities with coffee plantations. These crops are usually cultivated in organized rows or blocks, creating distinct spatial patterns that can closely resemble coffee in high-resolution imagery. Many are managed intensively for commercial production, and their canopy size, density, and layout make them frequent sources of confusion in visual interpretation and AI-based classification.

This section describes the visual characteristics of the most common plantation tree crops found in or near coffee-growing landscapes, highlighting the visual cues that help distinguish them from coffee. Those descriptions are followed by a series of visual examples.

Cocoa

Cocoa is often grown under partial shade, either in traditional agroforestry systems or in more organized plantations. The trees are small to medium in size and are typically planted in regular or semi-regular spacing. In high-resolution imagery, cocoa can look very similar to coffee.

Key distinguishing features include:

  • Slightly broader and more irregular crown shapes than coffee
  • More common in lower elevations and humid regions, especially in West Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of Latin America

Tea

Tea plantations consist of small trees that are frequently pruned, as harvesting involves picking mature leaves. Tea is often cultivated within agroforestry systems, where existing shade trees are kept when developing the tea plantation. The tea plants are typically grown in dense, continuous rows, creating a uniform pattern that is distinctly visible in high-resolution imagery. This planting arrangement closely resembles that of pruned coffee, making it challenging to differentiate between the two crops when they are grown in the same area.

Rubber

Rubber cultivation is characterized by tall trees with a dense canopy, which is notably thicker than that of coffee plantations. The trees are typically planted in organized rows, resulting in a clear and structured planting pattern visible in high-resolution imagery. However, rubber plantations can sometimes resemble coffee cultivation due to similar planting arrangements. Additionally, rubber trees exhibit strong phenological changes as they are deciduous (i.e., they shed their leaves seasonally). This phenology can lead to confusion with coffee plantations, particularly during certain growth stages or when both crops are grown in close proximity.

Banana

Banana and plantain plantations can resemble cocoa and coffee during their growing phase due to their similar canopy structure. However, as the plants reach maturity, they develop a distinct star-shaped canopy pattern, which serves as a key identifier. These plants reach maturity within a year and remain productive for three to four years, making them a common choice for providing shade to young coffee plants. Additionally, bananas and plantains are often used as intercrops even after coffee plantations reach maturity.

Coconut

Coconut palms are tall trees with large, fan-shaped leaves that form a distinct star-like pattern in imagery. They are typically spaced farther apart than coffee trees, and their tall, slender trunks cast long shadows in imagery. While their crown shape is distinctive, coconut plantations can still be confused with shaded coffee or intercropped systems if spacing and shadowing are unclear.

Oil palm

Oil palm plantations consist of medium to tall trees with wide, dense crowns arranged in highly regular planting grids. These plantations are highly structured and can appear similar to large-scale coffee monocultures, especially when young. The mature palms have a symmetrical star-like shape, often occurring in repeating patterns. However, in low-contrast or early-growth imagery, distinguishing oil palm from coffee can still be challenging.

Cashew

Cashew trees are medium-sized and often planted in semi-regular or loosely spaced patterns. Their canopy is generally broader and more open than coffee, with irregular shapes that vary across farms. In smallholder systems, cashew may appear similar to scattered coffee or agroforestry systems, particularly when intercropped or growing on sloped terrain. However, the larger crown size and less uniform spacing can help in distinguishing them.

item.title: Pruning Practices
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /cocoa_book/02_cocoa_cultivation/03_pruning/ -

Overview

Pruning is a key management practice in cocoa cultivation, essential for maintaining healthy trees and improving yields. It involves removing dead, diseased, or excess branches to allow more light into the canopy and to support balanced growth. In well-managed farms, pruning is typically carried out twice a year.

There are two main types of pruning:

  • Phytosanitary pruning removes dead or diseased branches to reduce pest and disease pressure.
  • Structural pruning shapes the tree to improve light penetration and air circulation, enhancing productivity and ease of harvest.

While most farmers prune to some extent, the quality of pruning can vary. In smallholder systems, pruning may be limited to removing lower branches, leaving the canopy dense; this type of pruning does not impact the appearance of cocoa trees in high-resolution imagery. In contrast, large plantations – such as those in Brazil or Ecuador – often contract out pruning tasks, resulting in more consistent and systematic canopy management.

These differences in pruning practices can affect how cocoa plots appear in high-resolution imagery, especially in terms of canopy uniformity.

item.title: Shade Management
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/03_shade_planting_patterns/ -

Overview

Coffee systems can be classified into five primary types based on their vertical and compositional diversity of shade:

  • Understory rustic polyculture
  • Traditional polyculture
  • Commercial polyculture
  • Shaded monoculture
  • Full sun monoculture.

These systems vary significantly in the amount of shade they provide, which can be broadly categorized as high, medium, low, or no shade. Rustic polyculture systems maintain an almost intact forest canopy, with minimal modifications to the understory, allowing coffee plants to grow in a natural, forest-like environment. These systems are typically classified as highly shaded and, from high-resolution imagery, closely resemble forests with a seemingly random distribution of large and small trees. This makes them particularly difficult to distinguish visually.

In contrast, traditional polyculture retains the forest canopy but replaces the understory with coffee plants. These systems provide a range of high to medium levels of shade and are also challenging to identify visually. However, the structured arrangement of coffee plants beneath the larger canopy trees can sometimes be discerned. Commercial polyculture takes a more intensive approach, removing both the natural canopy and understory and replacing them with coffee plants and smaller shade trees chosen for their commercial value. These systems generally provide medium to low levels of shade and are characterized by clear, structured patterns, often with orderly rows of coffee plants and shade trees. Shaded monoculture, a modernized system, eliminates the natural vegetation entirely, introducing leguminous trees specifically planted to create a shade canopy for coffee crops. Similar to commercial polyculture, these systems offer medium to low levels of shade and display highly organized layouts, often with alternating rows of shade trees and coffee plants. Finally, full sun monoculture removes all natural vegetation, replacing it entirely with coffee plants. This system provides no shade at all, resulting in an open and highly uniform planting structure.

item.title: Timber and Forests
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/01_coffee_gallery/02_confounding_samples/04_timber/ -

Overview

Though typically taller than coffee trees, timber plantations and natural forests – particularly degraded forests – can resemble coffee in satellite imagery, particularly when height information is not available. This describes the visual characteristics of timber and forest systems, then presents a series of visual examples.

Timber

Timber plantations are characterized by tall trees with a canopy structure that can appear very similar to coffee. However, the height of the trees often allows for shadows to be visible on the ground, which can help differentiate timber plantations from coffee systems. Timber plantations also exhibit a distinctive cycle of planting, growth, and harvesting that spans several years. This long-term cycle, evident in time-series imagery, provides a key indicator for distinguishing timber plantations from perennial coffee crops.

Pine

Pine plantations are typically very dense and – particularly in Brazil – can closely resemble coffee plantations. However, pine trees are taller than coffee plants, which makes their shadows more pronounced in imagery. Additionally, pine plantations often have a darker green canopy color than coffee. The planting pattern can also serve as an indicator, with pines generally spaced about seven meters apart, compared to the closer three-meter spacing typical of coffee.

Degraded forest

Degraded forests often resemble agroforestry coffee plantations due to their mix of a few remaining large trees and a layer of secondary vegetation. However, key indicators can help differentiate degraded forests from coffee plantations. Time-series imagery can reveal the gradual degradation process characteristic of forests, in contrast to the more deliberate planting and maintenance associated with coffee. Additionally, degraded forests tend to exhibit greater heterogeneity in canopy height compared to the relatively uniform canopy structure of coffee agroforestry systems. The absence of nearby farms or infrastructure commonly associated with agricultural activity can further indicate degraded forests rather than coffee plantations.

item.title: Intercropping Practices
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/04_intercrop/ -

Overview

Beyond agroforestry practices, coffee cultivation often incorporates a wide range of intercropping solutions that, while not providing shade, offer additional benefits such as supplementary income or enhanced soil management. In terms of ground cover, many systems practice weeding, leaving bare soil visible between coffee plants. However, in some cases, no weeding is performed, resulting in low vegetation (often grass) covering the soil between the trees, impacting the color in high-resolution imagery. Certain systems utilize intercropped cover crops, such as beans or maize, or cultivars that contribute to soil health and nitrogen fixation. Additionally, vine crops like black pepper are sometimes grown on poles arranged in rows between the coffee plants. Intercropped coffee systems tend to have a dense canopy with little to no visible soil in high-resolution imagery.

item.title: The Cocoa Life Cycle
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /cocoa_book/02_cocoa_cultivation/04_life_cycle/ -

Overview

Cocoa is a long-lived, perennial tree crop with a life cycle that can span several decades. Establishing a cocoa plantation requires careful early management, especially during the seedling stage, when trees are sensitive to light and moisture. Shade and sometimes irrigation are essential during this period, and cocoa is often interplanted with fast-growing crops like banana or cassava to provide early protection and income.

Cocoa trees typically become productive between two and five years after planting, depending on the variety. For instance, clonal types tend to fruit earlier and more uniformly than seed-grown trees. Once mature, trees remain productive for 20 to 25 years, although many are kept longer due to cultural preferences or economic constraints. As the trees mature, they produce pods that ripen throughout the year, changing color from dark green or purple to yellow, orange, or red, depending on the variety. This gradual change in canopy and pod coloration can affect how cocoa appears in satellite imagery, particularly in fields at different stages of maturity.
